title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: Give mirtify() code string, path .R file, unquoted inside { }: Three things happen: Model calls become mirt() calls model. ltm::rasch() estimates one common discrimination items, translation adds CONSTRAIN line rather using mirt’s itemtype = "Rasch" (fixes slopes 1 frees latent variance instead). Follow-calls fitted object translated . mirtify() remembers fit came rasch(), factor.scores(fit) becomes fscores() matching method (ltm’s empirical Bayes scores posterior modes, mirt calls MAP). difference gets note, written comment line. Turn notes = FALSE. Code involve packages left . Calls mirt equivalent kept comments, note use instead.
code: mirtify({   library(ltm)   fit <- rasch(LSAT)   summary(fit)   factor.scores(fit)   item.fit(fit) }) #> mirtify: 5 of 5 statements translated from ltm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # ltm::rasch() estimates one common discrimination for all items; the #> # CONSTRAIN line does the same in mirt. #> # ltm integrates over 21 Gauss-Hermite points and mirt over 61 points, so #> # estimates can differ slightly (usually in the second or third decimal). #> fit_model <- mirt.model("F = 1-5 #>                          CONSTRAIN = (1-5, a1)") #> fit <- mirt(LSAT, fit_model, itemtype = "2PL", SE = TRUE) #> # tidy() lists every parameter with its standard error, on the IRT scale. #> tidy(fit) #> # ltm's empirical Bayes scores are the posterior modes, which mirt calls MAP. #> # Like ltm, full.scores = FALSE returns one row per observed response #> # pattern; drop it to get one score per person. #> fscores(fit, method = "MAP", full.scores = FALSE) #> # Both use Yen's Q1-type chi-square with 10 ability groups, but the groups #> # are formed differently, so the statistics differ a little. fit_stats = #> # "S_X2" is usually preferred in mirt. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "X2")

title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: eRm estimates Rasch models conditional maximum likelihood (CML), mirt uses marginal maximum likelihood (MML) normal latent trait. Rasch family two give similar item estimates. eRm reports item easiness (minus difficulty) centred sum zero, translated coef() summary() calls convert mirt’s difficulties form. Andersen’s likelihood-ratio test (LRtest()) becomes comparison mirt: model equal item parameters low high score groups one separate parameters. raschdat1 eRm gives LR = 32.5 29 df (p = .30) translation gives 32.8 29 df (p = .29).
code: mirtify({   library(eRm)   fit <- RM(raschdat1)   coef(fit)   pp <- person.parameter(fit)   itemfit(pp)   LRtest(fit)   plotPImap(fit) }) #> mirtify: 7 of 7 statements translated from eRm #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # eRm uses conditional maximum likelihood (CML); mirt uses marginal maximum #> # likelihood with a normal latent trait, so estimates are close but not #> # identical. #> # eRm reports item easiness (beta = -difficulty) centred to sum to zero; #> # coef() and summary() below convert mirt's difficulties to the same form. #> fit <- mirt(raschdat1, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", SE = TRUE) #> # eRm's item easiness is minus the difficulty, centred to sum to zero. #> fit_b <- coef(fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "b"] #> -(fit_b - mean(fit_b)) #> # eRm's person parameters are maximum likelihood estimates. For all-correct #> # or all-wrong patterns mirt returns -Inf or Inf where eRm extrapolates; #> # method = "WLE" gives finite values for everyone. #> pp <- fscores(fit, method = "ML", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # mirt's infit and outfit mean squares use EAP person estimates while eRm #> # uses ML estimates, so values differ a little. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "infit") #> # Andersen's test compares item parameters across score groups. Here the same #> # comparison is a likelihood-ratio test between a model with equal item #> # parameters in both groups and one with separate parameters. It uses #> # marginal rather than conditional likelihood, so the statistic differs from #> # eRm's. #> fit_score <- rowSums(raschdat1, na.rm = TRUE) #> fit_split <- ifelse(fit_score > median(fit_score), "high", "low") #> fit_free <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                           itemtype = "Rasch") #> fit_equal <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                            itemtype = "Rasch", #>                            invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> anova(fit_equal, fit_free) #> # gg_wright() draws the person-item map with ggplot2. #> gg_wright(fit)

what: TAM: Q matrices, groups and latent regression
title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: tam.mml() tam.mml.2pl() translate used arguments: Q matrix becomes mirt.model() correlated dimensions, group becomes multipleGroup() equal item parameters free group means variances, Y becomes mirt’s latent regression (covdata formula), pweights becomes survey.weights.
code: mirtify("library(TAM)          mod <- tam.mml(resp, Q = Q)          mod2 <- tam.mml.2pl(resp, group = school)          wle <- tam.wle(mod)          wle$WLE.rel          tam.modelfit(mod)          IRT.compareModels(mod, mod2)") #> mirtify: 7 of 7 statements translated from TAM #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # Like TAM, itemtype = "Rasch" fixes the slopes at 1, sets the latent mean to #> # 0 and estimates the latent variance. #> # mirt.model() builds the same between-item structure from TAM's Q matrix, #> # with correlated dimensions. #> # TAM integrates over 21 nodes from -6 to 6 and mirt over 61 points, so #> # estimates can differ slightly. #> mod_model <- mirt.model(Q, COV = upper.tri(diag(ncol(Q)))) #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, itemtype = "Rasch", SE = TRUE) #> # For polytomous items use itemtype = "gpcm", which is what TAM fits for #> # them. #> # As in TAM, the latent variance is fixed at 1 and every item has its own #> # slope. #> # With group, TAM keeps item parameters equal across groups and estimates a #> # mean and variance for each group; multipleGroup() with this invariance does #> # the same. #> mod2 <- multipleGroup(resp, 1, group = school, itemtype = "2PL", #>                       SE = TRUE, #>                       invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> # Warm's weighted likelihood estimates, as in tam.wle(). #> wle <- fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> empirical_rxx(wle) #> # M2() gives the overall fit test with RMSEA and SRMSR. For TAM's Q3 #> # statistics use residuals(mod, type = "Q3") or gg_q3(mod). #> M2(mod) #> # anova() compares nested mirt models with AIC, BIC and a likelihood-ratio #> # test. #> anova(mod, mod2)

what: irtQ: the scaling constant D and priors
title: Moving from ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ to mirt
text: irtQ often uses D = 1.702, multiplies every slope. mirt D, slopes equal irtQ’s times 1.702. translated summary() coef() calls divide back. translation also keeps irtQ’s defaults mirt share: 49 quadrature points -6 6, one shared slope 1PLM items, Beta(5, 16) prior guessing parameters.
code: mirtify("library(irtQ)          mod <- est_irt(data = resp, D = 1.702,                         model = c('1PLM', '1PLM', '3PLM', '3PLM', 'GRM'),                         cats = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 4))          summary(mod)          est_score(mod, method = 'WL')          sx2_fit(mod)") #> mirtify: 5 of 5 statements translated from irtQ #>  #> # mirtverse loads mirt, so one library() call covers both. #> library(mirtverse) #> # irtQ's 1PLM items share one estimated slope; the CONSTRAIN line does the #> # same in mirt. #> # irtQ puts a Beta(5, 16) prior on the guessing parameters by default; the #> # PRIOR line does the same in mirt. #> # With guessing parameters the likelihood can have more than one peak, so #> # mirt and irtQ can stop at slightly different estimates. Compare the #> # log-likelihoods if the estimates differ. #> # quadpts and theta_lim use irtQ's quadrature (49 points from -6 to 6). #> # irtQ multiplies the slopes by D = 1.702; mirt does not. mirt's slopes equal #> # irtQ's times 1.702, and coef() and summary() below rescale them. #> mod_model <- mirt.model("F = 1-5 #>                          CONSTRAIN = (1-2, a1) #>                          PRIOR = (3-4, g, expbeta, 5, 16)") #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, #>             itemtype = c(rep("2PL", 2), rep("3PL", 2), "graded"), #>             quadpts = 49, theta_lim = c(-6, 6), SE = TRUE) #> mod_pars <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items #> mod_pars[, "a"] <- mod_pars[, "a"] / 1.702  # irtQ's slopes include D = 1.702 #> mod_pars #> fscores(mod, method = "WLE", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # Orlando and Thissen's S-X2, as in irtQ. #> itemfit(mod, fit_stats = "S_X2")

Philip Chalmers, one comprehensive open-source packages item response theory. introduced Journal Statistical Software (Chalmers, 2012) developed continuously since, version 1.48 released CRAN October 2026. widely used research educational psychological measurement. mirt can: Estimate wide range models: unidimensional multidimensional, exploratory confirmatory, bifactor two-tier, 30 item types (Rasch, 2PL 4PL, graded response, (generalized) partial credit, nominal, ideal-point, nonparametric spline items ), plus user-defined items. Handle complex designs: multiple-group analysis measurement invariance, mixed-effects explanatory IRT (mixedmirt()), latent class diagnostic classification models (mdirt()). Use several estimation engines: EM fixed quasi-Monte Carlo quadrature, Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro (MHRM) algorithm high-dimensional models, several standard-error methods. For all-correct #> # or all-wrong patterns mirt returns -Inf or Inf where eRm extrapolates; #> # method = "WLE" gives finite values for everyone. #> pp <- fscores(fit, method = "ML", full.scores.SE = TRUE) #> # mirt's infit and outfit mean squares use EAP person estimates while eRm #> # uses ML estimates, so values differ a little. #> itemfit(fit, fit_stats = "infit") #> # Andersen's test compares item parameters across score groups. Here the same #> # comparison is a likelihood-ratio test between a model with equal item #> # parameters in both groups and one with separate parameters. It uses #> # marginal rather than conditional likelihood, so the statistic differs from #> # eRm's. #> fit_score <- rowSums(raschdat1, na.rm = TRUE) #> fit_split <- ifelse(fit_score > median(fit_score), "high", "low") #> fit_free <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                           itemtype = "Rasch") #> fit_equal <- multipleGroup(raschdat1, 1, group = fit_split, #>                            itemtype = "Rasch", #>                            invariance = c("slopes", "intercepts", "free_means", "free_var")) #> anova(fit_equal, fit_free)  mirtify("mod <- irtQ::est_irt(data = resp, D = 1.702, model = '3PLM')") #> mirtify: 1 of 1 statements translated from irtQ #>  #> library(mirtverse) #> # irtQ puts a Beta(5, 16) prior on the guessing parameters by default; the #> # PRIOR line does the same in mirt. #> # With guessing parameters the likelihood can have more than one peak, so #> # mirt and irtQ can stop at slightly different estimates. Compare the #> # log-likelihoods if the estimates differ. #> # quadpts and theta_lim use irtQ's quadrature (49 points from -6 to 6). #> # irtQ multiplies the slopes by D = 1.702; mirt does not. mirt's slopes equal #> # irtQ's times 1.702, and coef() and summary() below rescale them. #> mod_model <- mirt.model(sprintf("F = 1-%1$d #>                                  PRIOR = (1-%1$d, g, expbeta, 5, 16)", ncol(resp))) #> mod <- mirt(resp, mod_model, itemtype = "3PL", quadpts = 49, #>             theta_lim = c(-6, 6), SE = TRUE)
